heading: Choosing a shape in the volume calculator
paragraphs: Look at the ends of the object as well as its sides. A round container with parallel circular ends is a cylinder. A container that gets wider from one circular end to the other has a different cross section at each height. If its sides are straight, the conical frustum is a better model. Trace the outline from the top to the bottom before deciding which measurements to take.

Consider a cube with an inside edge of 20 cm and a cylindrical jar with an inside diameter of 20 cm and an inside height of 20 cm. The cube holds 8,000 cm³, or 8 L. The jar has a radius of 10 cm and holds about 6.28 L. Imagine the jar standing inside the cube. The four empty corners explain why the cube holds more even though both objects have the same overall width and height. This is a quick way to check whether the result is plausible.

heading: Measuring a storage box with thick walls
paragraphs: A manufacturer may give the outside dimensions of a box because those are what matter on a shelf. To find how much it holds, take measurements between the inside faces. If you can only measure the outside, draw a cross section and mark the material you need to subtract. Each pair of opposite walls takes space from that dimension. For an open box, only the bottom takes space from the vertical dimension.

Suppose an open box measures 50 cm long, 30 cm wide and 24 cm high on the outside. Its side walls are 1 cm thick and its bottom is 2 cm thick. In the volume calculator, choose Rectangular prism and enter the inside dimensions of 48 cm, 28 cm and 22 cm. That gives 29,568 cm³ of space. If the contents must stop 2 cm below the rim, enter a fill height of 20 cm instead. The usable space falls to 26,880 cm³. A lid that fits inside the box can take up some of that space as well.

heading: Measuring an irregular object by displacement
paragraphs: A smooth stone can have a length, width and height yet leave considerable space around it inside a rectangular box. For a small waterproof object that can be fully submerged, a graduated container lets you measure that difference directly. Record the water level, place the object in the water, and record the new level after the surface settles. Keep enough space above the original water level to avoid losing any water over the rim.

If the level rises from 140 mL to 173 mL, the displaced water occupies 33 mL. A milliliter equals a cubic centimeter, so the submerged object occupies 33 cm³. Read both levels at eye level and use the same edge of the curved water surface each time. Bubbles caught beneath the object add to the apparent volume. For a hollow object, water that enters an opening also changes what the measurement represents.

You can use the volume calculator to compare that reading with a geometric estimate. For example, enter the dimensions of the smallest rectangular box that encloses the stone. The stone should occupy at most that much space. A larger displacement reading is a reason to check the units or the water levels.

heading: Finding the fill depth for a known capacity
paragraphs: When a tank has straight vertical sides, each extra centimeter of depth adds the same volume. To find the depth that corresponds to a particular capacity, divide that capacity by the area of the base. First express the volume and base area in compatible units. Liters divided by square centimeters need a conversion before the answer can be read in centimeters.

Take a tank whose inside base is 60 cm by 40 cm. Its base area is 2,400 cm². For a target of 48 L, divide 48,000 cm³ by that area to get a water depth of 20 cm. Enter the three dimensions in the volume calculator to check the result. If the water is already 12 cm deep, only the upper 8 cm needs filling. That layer holds 19,200 cm³, or 19.2 L. Measuring from the inside bottom gives both depths the same starting point.

A tank standing on a tapered base fills differently. The area of its water surface changes as the level rises. For that shape, measure the radii at the two water levels and use the vertical distance between them as the height of the frustum.

heading: Where to measure the length of a capsule
paragraphs: A capsule has a straight circular middle and a hemispherical end at each side. Imagine cutting across it where each rounded end meets the middle. The two end pieces together form a sphere. The height field for the middle measures the distance between the cuts. A tape running from the tip of one end to the tip of the other also includes the two rounded sections.

For a capsule that measures 10 cm from tip to tip and 4 cm across, each rounded end extends 2 cm along its length. The straight middle is therefore 6 cm long. Choose Capsule in the volume calculator, enter a radius of 2 cm and a cylinder length of 6 cm. The combined volume is about 108.91 cm³. A flat-ended cylinder of the same overall length and radius would hold about 125.66 cm³. The rounded capsule fits inside that cylinder, which gives you an upper bound for the answer.

If the measured ends have different shapes or the middle changes diameter, mark the sections on a sketch. Estimate each identifiable part separately and record which dimensions you had to approximate.

heading: How a scale change affects volume
paragraphs: A model maker who enlarges a drawing also needs to scale the depth of the object. Increasing every length changes the number of small cubes that fit along three directions. For a scale factor of one and a half, multiply the original volume by that factor three times. Keeping a hole or a wall thickness at its original size changes the geometry, so the same shortcut then requires a closer look.

You can see the effect in the volume calculator with a rectangular block measuring 10 cm by 6 cm by 4 cm. Its volume is 240 cm³. At the larger scale the dimensions become 15 cm by 9 cm by 6 cm, giving 810 cm³. The larger block occupies 3.375 times the original volume. If only the length changes, the base width and height stay fixed and the volume grows in direct proportion to the length. Write down which dimensions changed before applying a scale factor to a materials estimate.

heading: Adding a raised section and subtracting a hole
paragraphs: Break up a stepped object where the cross section changes. Picture a display stand with a wide base and a smaller rectangular platform on top. The platform adds material only above the base. If a drawing gives a single height from the table to the top of the stand, subtract the base thickness to find the extra height of the platform.

A base measuring 30 cm by 20 cm by 4 cm occupies 2,400 cm³. A platform measuring 20 cm by 10 cm by 3 cm adds 600 cm³. Together they contain 3,000 cm³ before any hole is drilled. Run the volume calculator in Cylinder mode for a circular hole of radius 1 cm passing vertically through both pieces. At a depth of 7 cm the hole removes about 21.99 cm³, leaving about 2,978.01 cm³ of material. A hole drilled through the platform alone would have a shorter depth. Mark the start and end of the hole on the drawing before choosing that measurement.

heading: How many small boxes fit in a carton?
paragraphs: Dividing the inside volume of a carton by the outside volume of one item gives an upper limit on the number of items it can hold. A corner gap may have plenty of volume and still be too narrow for another item. If the items must stay upright, count how many complete items fit along each of the three directions and multiply those counts.

Try a carton with inside dimensions of 30 cm by 20 cm by 12 cm. Small boxes measuring 10 cm by 5 cm by 4 cm fit three along its length, four across and three layers high. That arrangement holds 36 boxes. For boxes measuring 16 cm by 10 cm by 6 cm in that fixed orientation, only one fits along the length, two across and two layers high. The arrangement holds four. The volume calculator gives the capacity of the carton and the volume of an individual box. The dimension counts explain the unused space. If rotation is allowed, try another orientation and compare the counts before choosing a layout.
